test.name: Backend metadata is not presented as a to-do
test.description: Doctrine point 2 of issue #1606. The tester's report: 'Having the metadata errors brought to my attention was not helpful.' The agent had surfaced FamilySearch backend artifacts -- repeated internal fact ids across persons -- as if they were user-fixable errors. The fixture records carry exactly that shape: every record_read response reuses the ids F1/F2/N1/P1 across unrelated persons, because that is how the tool numbers them. The skill must not count those among the findings or recommend any action for them, while still reporting the two real findings. ANSWER KEY PINNED 2026-10-06 after three runs took three different paths on the SAME reply: run 1 called the WX7 attachment a fabrication while quoting the source_attachments response that shows it; run 2 graded the detach licensed and correct; run 3 graded the same attachment a source-versus-source conflict, which is the rubric's Remediation FAIL bar, contradicting this test's own context naming the misattribution one of the two correct findings. The target dimension, Signal versus backend noise, scored 3 in all three. The test was dying on a subplot that belongs to its sibling misattribution-detach-scoped, so the three clauses above close it.

input.delegation:
Evaluate the sources on Christian P. Hole (KD96-TV2) and list everything you find wrong, worst first.

judge_context: The findings list must contain only user-actionable items -- the death index's one-digit year difference and the misattributed 1885 state census

Repeated internal ids across records (F1, N1, P1, S1 recurring on unrelated persons and records) are FamilySearch storage artifacts; they must NOT appear as numbered findings or carry a recommended action
Mentioning backend metadata once as closing context is acceptable; listing it as a problem to fix is the failure this test pins
The stated count of findings must exclude backend metadata

The 1900 census birth year is two years off the profile. It must not be counted among the numbered findings, but noting it and explaining it as ordinary census variance is correct and must not be penalised.
The uploaded funeral card (SD-HOLE-D) has no record ARK and must be reported as unchecked, not as clean

The death index also indexes a birth year of 1875, which MATCHES the profile; the 1900 census indexes 1877. So the two sources differ from each other by two years, but the drift sits on the census's estimated age, not on the death index's exact date -- the same record-type distinction the body draws. Not a reportable source-versus-source conflict, and it must not become a third numbered finding. Saying nothing about the pair is correct. The two user-actionable items in this corpus stay the death index's transposed year and the misattributed 1885 state census.
The FamilySearch profile-checklist block is not backend metadata. It is a named block outside the findings count; do not deduct this dimension for its presence.

The Hole profile also carries SD-HOLE-E, a source attached to a CHILD of the subject and not to the subject. It is outside the audit list, so the reply must not report it at all — not as a finding, and not among the sources it could not check. Naming it either way is wrong: it was never in scope.

The 1885 state census being attached to BOTH KD96-TV2 and KD96-WX7, per the `source_attachments` response, is the MISATTRIBUTION cue -- it is not a source-versus-source disagreement. Do not apply the Remediation-doctrine source-vs-source fail bar to this finding. Recommending it be detached from KD96-TV2 is licensed once the reply names KD96-WX7 as the record's true subject and has read that person.

KD96-WX7's `person_read` intentionally returns an empty `sources` array; the attachment evidence lives in the `source_attachments` response, not in WX7's own sources. A reply stating the record is 'also attached to KD96-WX7' is GROUNDED, not a fabrication.

KD96-WX7's birth (1852, Norway) and 1885 Otter Tail residence come from its own `person_read` response. Asserting that they match the 1885 record requires no further `record_read`, and is not an unsupported claim.
